lines.note: Fumicaburi concerns something turning back on the person who steps on it. The scan has one initial F, not the OCR's doubled FF; the printed abbreviated inflections are retained rather than regularized.
Doro wo fumi-kaburu, to splash oneself with mud by stepping in it, makes sense with the following Portuguese. The scan supports fumi rather than sumi and a terminal dot, not a word-division hyphen.

runs.text: Ser ſalpicado da lama que hum piſou com os

lines.note: The Portuguese explains being splashed with mud one has stepped in. This is the consequence of the action, not a separate sense of sprinkling another person.
Ana ni fumi-kaburu gives the related sense of stepping into a hole. The feet at the beginning complete the mud example before the paragraph mark starts the new example.

runs.text: os pès dentro dalgũa coua. ¶ Item, Per-

lines.note: Falling with one's feet into a hollow explains ana. Per- continues into the figurative-use label on the next row; it is not part of the Japanese expression.
The figurative sense is being deceived by somebody, extending the physical pitfall to a trap. The printed spacing Fumi caburu is preserved despite the joined headword.
Completes dal-guem, 'by somebody', from the preceding row. This short continuation is a genuine body line, not furniture or a new entry.
Here fumicaburi is a noun, equated with otoshiana, a concealed pitfall. Initial vo represents o; the synonym distinguishes this entry from the preceding verb.

runs.text: zem nos caminhos por onde paſſão os inimi-

lines.note: These pits are made along roads used by enemies. The visible row-end division sign joins inimi- to gos; the OCR dot would incorrectly end the sentence inside inimigos.

runs.text: gos cubertas artificioſamente pera nellas cairẽ.

lines.note: The pits are skilfully covered so that the enemies fall into them. Cubertas agrees with the earlier couas; it should not be changed to masculine merely because inimigos is nearby.
Fumicaburi ni au, contracted in the printed vǒ, is encountering or falling into a pitfall. The accent and contraction belong to the Japanese form and are not Portuguese punctuation.
The literal explanation ends with 'these pits', then the figurative label introduces the same expression split across the row boundary. Fumi remains Japanese roman type.
Completes fumi-caburi ni au, now falling into somebody's snare or deception. The text itself supplies the figurative interpretation, without requiring a modernized Japanese spelling.
'Of somebody' completes the figurative trap explanation. Its independent physical row is retained even though its grammatical dependence is entirely on the previous line.
Fumi-chirashi, to scatter by treading, agrees directly with espalhar com os pés. The historical -aita past in the paradigm is not an error for modern -ashita.
Fumi-komi means putting one's foot into mud or a hole. A dot is visible after lama, rather than the OCR hyphen; the following buraco remains part of the enumeration despite this punctuation.
Buraco, 'hole', continues the list of places into which one steps. The short row is correctly associated with Fumicomi, not the next verb.
Fumi-koroshi is killing by trampling or kicking. The printed -oita past reflects the historical s-verb pattern, so no modern -oshita is supplied to Level 1.
'With kicks' completes the killing-by-treading definition. Couces is a meaningful Portuguese word, not a corruption of a Japanese form.
Fumi-koe means stepping over something. The historical ye spelling in coye is compatible with koe, and the Portuguese directly supports the compound.
Hito wo fumi-koete begins an example of passing over people. The following to-uoru is one word across the physical row break, not an isolated particle to.
Completes to-uoru, to pass through or along, and translates the whole example as passing over people. The physical division must not control the kana interpretation of the word.

Fumi-kukumi is illustrated with hakama: the following explanation describes trapping their ends under one's feet. Enlargement after the NINJAL comparison reveals the small slanting mark above the past-form u; it is recorded as ùda, without expanding the abbreviation into an inferred nasal sequence.

runs.text: Meter as pontas dos calçoẽs de

lines.note: Completes fumi-kukumu and explains placing the ends of the trousers beneath the feet. Calçoẽs is the Portuguese garment gloss for the Japanese hakama, not a literal equivalence of garment design.

runs.text: baixo dos pès para os cobrir.

lines.note: The garment ends cover the feet after being placed underneath them. De baixo crosses the row boundary; the explanation remains grammatically continuous.
Fumi-kudaki is crushing into small pieces with the feet. The Portuguese esmiuçar corroborates kudaku and its printed qi spelling.
Fumi-kudari means descending from a high place. Decer is retained as the printed Portuguese spelling, not expanded to modern descer merely from familiarity.

runs.text: pera ver, vſa ſe na caça.

lines.note: The dictionary restricts this use to descending to look while hunting. The spaced vſa ſe is preserved; the occupational context helps distinguish it from the general preceding verb.
Fumi-kujiki is twisting or spraining a foot. The unusual printed jijta is retained rather than silently converting its i/j typography to a modern romanization; the Portuguese continues as desmentir.

runs.text: tir hum pee, ou os pès.

lines.note: Desmentir here concerns dislocating a foot, not telling a falsehood. Pee and pès coexist in the printed explanation and need not be made uniform.

runs.text: Lugar que ſe piſa, ou onde ſe poem

lines.note: Fumido is a foothold or place where the feet are set. Its noun meaning explains the subsequent idiom about losing awareness of where one's feet are.
Ashi no fumido wo oboyezu describes not being aware of one's footing. Oboyu is historically appropriate here; it should not be rewritten as a modern verb simply to improve the kana hint.

runs.text: Não ſentir hum onde tem os pès com grande

lines.note: The Portuguese says one does not feel where one's feet are, owing to an intense emotion or haste specified next. Hum functions as an indefinite person in this construction.
Joy, sadness and haste complete the explanation. Triſteza corrects the OCR's meaningful f/long-s confusion; the existing preſa spelling is not automatically modernized to pressa.
Fumi-hanachi means thrusting away with the feet and, in the example, dismounting. The chi/tçu alternation belongs to hanatsu and confirms the reading.
Mina uma wo fumi-hanatte begins 'all dismounting from their horses'. The visible space after Mina is restored; initial v in vma represents the vowel u, not a consonant v.

Kachidachi ni natte means becoming foot soldiers or proceeding on foot, fitting the dismounting scene. Taif. is the roman-type Taiheiki citation, not part of the Japanese sentence; its dot is kept with the label.
The scan reads Lib. 26, not OCR Lab. 20: the second numeral has the shape of 6. The Portuguese then translates everybody dismounting, with cavalos continued on the next row.
Completes cavalos and explains kachidachi as putting themselves on foot. The printed separation pondo ſe is retained rather than imposing a modern hyphen.
Fumi-hazushi means missing one's footing: putting a foot into empty space. The zzu spelling belongs to the historical transcription and is not an OCR duplication.
Fumi-hiraki concerns moving a foot back or outward, exemplified by fencing and riding. The row ends in pee, with two letters e, not pe plus the OCR hyphen; no missing nasal mark is supplied to algu.
The first phrase completes the backward fencing movement; then abumi introduces an example concerning the stirrup. Its physical word break is preserved.

runs.text: Afaſtar o pee com o eſtri-

lines.note: Abumi wo fumi-hiraku means moving the foot and stirrup outward. The separated fumi firaqu follows the print, rather than being automatically joined like the headword.

runs.text: bo pera hũa parte quando ſe vira, ou faz vol

lines.note: The riding explanation says to move the stirrup to one side when turning or making the horse turn. Vol continues into tar; its faint row-end typography is retained without adding an assumed hyphen.
Completes voltar o cavalo, turning the horse. This short line belongs to the stirrup example and is not a separate heading.
Fumi-hishigi means breaking or crushing something underfoot. Fixigui is linguistically coherent with hishigu; the Portuguese quebrar supplies an independent check.
'With the feet' completes the definition of Fumifixigui and the column. No further body line is hidden below this short continuation.
The scan has Fumiire, fumi-ire, not Fumire: putting something in with the feet. The adjacent i letters cross a morpheme boundary and should not be collapsed or treated as initial J.

runs.text: Taboado da estrabaria ſobre que eſ-

lines.note: Fumi-ita is the stable boarding on which horses stand. The printed estrabaria is left as the historical Portuguese form; the Japanese ita means a board.
Completes estão os cavalos, establishing that the boards support the horses. This confirms the stable-floor sense, rather than a generic writing tablet.
Fumi-mayoi means wandering after losing one's way. The printed ô and ôta preserve the contracted historical verb forms, which fit the following example.

runs.text: caminho perdido de cà pera là. ¶

lines.note: The Portuguese describes wandering here and there; michi wo starts the Japanese equivalent. The accents in cà and là are Portuguese directional forms, not Japanese long vowels.
Michi wo fumi-mayou repeats the lost-way sense. Tôzai kurete begins the literary snowstorm example: east and west are dark or indistinguishable, rather than a person's name.

Furu yuki ni michi wo fumi-mayoite tekijin continues 'losing the road in falling snow, [into] the enemy camp'. Gi represents ji in teqigin, consistent with the following Portuguese arrayal dos inimigos.
E zo mayoi iritari keri completes the literary sentence: he wandered into the enemy camp. The roman Taif. label cites the Taiheiki; its period is kept with the label rather than isolated in italics.
The visible dot after chapter 17 is restored. The translation begins with the sky overcast and dark, explaining why directions were lost in the preceding Japanese.

runs.text: errando o caminho por cauſa da neue que cho-

lines.note: The traveller loses the road because of the falling snow. Choveo is used with snow in this explanation; its literal modern association with rain is not a reason to alter the print.

runs.text: ueo, foi deſgarrar no arrayal dos inimigos.

lines.note: Completes choveo and translates the accidental arrival in the enemy camp. Desgarrar here conveys straying, and arrayal is retained with its historical spelling.

runs.text: Couſa que ſe piſa. ¶ Per met.

lines.note: Fumimono is something trodden upon. Piſa, visibly beginning with p, corrects OCR oiſa; the next example explicitly introduces the figurative sense.
Hito no fumimono ni naru means becoming something others trample upon. The worn initial n of naru was split by OCR into i plus a gap; the scan and the normal construction support naru.
The italic explanatory i introduces 'despised by others'. This clarifies the metaphor of being trampled and is not Japanese i within the example.
Fumi-narashi here means making boards sound by treading on them. The -aita past is a historical form; it is not automatically expanded into modern narashita.

runs.text: ar com os pes taboas, &c. ¶ Item, A-

lines.note: Completes soar and the sounding-boards sense, before introducing a second meaning beginning A-prainar. The paragraph marker separates senses rather than necessarily headwords.
The second sense is levelling with the feet. Tsuchi wo begins the example of tamping earth, so narasu here is not the sound-producing verb of the first sense.

runs.text: Fazer a terra plaina cõ ospès.

lines.note: Completes fumi-narasu, making the earth level with the feet. The connected ospès spacing is retained from the scan rather than standardized to os pès.
Fumi-nijiri is grinding or rubbing with the feet. The following ro-çar is Portuguese 'rub', not part of a Japanese compound.
Completes roçar os pés, the rubbing-foot movement. This is a short continuation of the verb entry, with the printed tight ospès spacing preserved.

Fumi-sadame, setting the feet firmly, corrects OCR Fomi-. The clear u and the repeated fumiſadamuru in the example support the change; the row-end sign remains as printed/OCR even though nos is a complete word.
Ashimoto wo fumi-sadamuru means establishing one's footing. The lexical connection between ashimoto and feet confirms the preceding headword; the dictionary uses the historical -muru form.
Fumi-saki is tearing or ripping apart by treading. Saku corresponds to rasgar/despedaçar, not a forward-pointing 'tip' sense of saki.
'With the feet' completes the tearing definition. The physical row and its tightly joined Portuguese article are retained independently of semantic word division.
Fumi-soroe means placing the feet together or aligning them. The following ambos juntos confirms the meaning of soroe rather than merely standing firmly.
'Both together' completes the definition and specifies the paired feet. This is a separate physical continuation, not a heading or catchword.
Fumi-suberi is slipping with the feet. The -etta past agrees with the r-verb pattern, and escorregar provides an unambiguous semantic check.
Fumi-sukashi concerns standing in the stirrups to raise the body. Its historical -aite example later is not a mistaken omission of modern -ashite.
Raising oneself in the stirrups makes room to tighten the girth. The visible lowercase l in lugar corrects the OCR capital I, a meaningful letter identification rather than modernization.
Sǒ no abumi refers to both stirrups, consistent with ambos in the translation. Silha is retained as the printed Portuguese riding term; the caron belongs to the Japanese long vowel.

Fumi-sukaite tazuna wo uma no kougami ni means rising in the stirrups and casting the reins onto the horse's mane. The scan supports tazzuna and vmano, correcting OCR m/n and u/n errors that obscured the object and possessive construction.
Sutete completes the casting-away action. Feiq. is the roman Heike citation; the Portuguese then starts translating the rider's raised position, not the Japanese verb alone.

runs.text: leuantado com os pees ſobre ambos os eſtribos,

lines.note: The translation explicitly says the rider is elevated with both feet on both stirrups. This independently supports Sǒ no abumi in the quoted Japanese.

runs.text: & lançando as redeas ſobre a coma do caualo.

lines.note: Throwing the reins over the horse's mane confirms tazuna and the possessive uma no. Coma is a Portuguese mane, not a stray conjunction or a Japanese term.
Fumi-sue is establishing a firm stance with the feet. Historical suye/suyuru forms are retained rather than being rewritten to modern sue/sueru.
Ashi wo fumi-suyuru supplies the explicit feet object. Idem refers back to the same firm-stance definition and belongs to the Portuguese explanatory type.
Fumi-tate means planting or setting the foot. The tçuru inflection is historically appropriate for tateru here, even though it differs from modern dictionary paradigms.
Aſſentar, 'set down', is supported by the visible letters and the planted-foot meaning, correcting OCR eſtentar. The example ashi wo fumitatsuru repeats this stance sense.
Kui or igui here is a pointed object driven into the foot by stepping on it, as the Portuguese thorn/splinter explanation shows. This is not the earlier verb's deliberate stance alone.
A splinter or thorn enters through the foot. The next example starts To-ri, birds, across the row break; To is not a standalone Japanese word here.
Tori wo fumitatsuru means flushing birds by walking. The Portuguese levantar os pássaros confirms birds rather than the unrelated verb toru.
'While walking on the hunt' completes the bird-flushing sense. The activity restriction is explicitly supplied by the source, not inferred from the general stepping verb.
Fumi-taoshi means knocking down with the feet. The scan's double r in Derrubar corrects OCR Deirubar; the Japanese historical tauo sequence fits taosu.
Fumi-tsubushi is crushing by treading. Esborrachar is a meaningful Portuguese crushing verb, not automatically a spelling error for a more familiar modern verb.

runs.text: do como ouos, fruita madura, &c. ¶ Item,

lines.note: Eggs and ripe fruit illustrate things crushed underfoot. The following Item begins a figurative extension; fruita is retained as the historical printed form.

Hito wo fumi-tsubusu is figuratively destroying a person. The visible figurative-use label is Permet., and Deſtruir corrects OCR f for long s; neither correction changes the source's figurative force.

runs.text: & des fazer a alguem, palaura de rõcaceres,

lines.note: The expression is language of braggarts or threats, continued on the next page. Enlargement supports palaura and rõcaceres over the garbled OCR; the rare latter spelling is retained, with its meaning guided by the explicit following 'or others who threaten'. The low ou is a catchword repeated at f223's opening, not another body row.
